4	      deadline of August 3, 2026 (10.5 weeks), we adopt a two-tier approach. The CORE
5	      SUBMISSION targets 2 models (Qwen3-235B-A22B + Llama 4 Scout) × 20 typologically
6	      diverse languages × all 5 transfer conditions, producing all three core contributions.
7	      The CAMERA-READY EXTENSION adds Gemma 4 31B Dense as a third architecture +
8	      30+ additional languages. This is scientifically justified: 2 models already
9	      provide architectural contrast (94-layer MoE vs. 48-layer MoE), while the third
10	      (60-layer dense) strengthens but is not essential for the core claims. LANGUAGE
11	      SELECTION: Following Ploeger et al.''s (Computational Linguistics, 2025) principled
12	      framework for typologically diverse language selection, we select 20 languages
13	      across 3 resource tiers and 10+ language families, constrained to the intersection
14	      of GlobalMMLU, Belebele, and MMLU-ProX availability: HIGH-RESOURCE (6): Chinese
15	      (zh), Spanish (es), French (fr), German (de), Japanese (ja), Arabic (ar) — covering
16	      Sino-Tibetan, Romance, Germanic, Japonic, Afro-Asiatic; MID-RESOURCE (7): Hindi
17	      (hi), Russian (ru), Korean (ko), Turkish (tr), Vietnamese (vi), Thai (th), Indonesian
18	      (id) — covering Indo-Aryan, Slavic, Koreanic, Turkic, Austroasiatic, Kra-Dai,
19	      Austronesian; LOW-RESOURCE (7): Swahili (sw), Bengali (bn), Telugu (te), Khmer
20	      (km), Yoruba (yo), Amharic (am), Burmese (my) — covering Bantu, Indo-Aryan,
21	      Dravidian, Austroasiatic, Niger-Congo, Semitic, Sino-Tibetan. This selection
22	      maximizes typological diversity (word order, morphological type, script diversity)
23	      while ensuring benchmark coverage and enabling fine-grained resource-tier analysis.
24	      MINIMAL VIABLE EXPERIMENT (MVE) — 8-WEEK PLAN: Phase A — Infrastructure & Activation
25	      Extraction (weeks 1-2): Set up extraction pipeline. Extract activations for
26	      Qwen3-235B-A22B at every 4th layer (24 probed layers across 94 total) and Llama
27	      4 Scout at every 4th layer (12 probed layers across 48 total) on English MMLU/ARC-Challenge

29	      GlobalMMLU''s matched questions. INT8 validation ablation for Llama 4 Scout
30	      on 5% random subset comparing INT8 vs. FP16 at 5 representative layers. Phase
31	      B — Probe Training & Transfer Experiments (weeks 3-5): Train logistic regression
32	      + 2-layer MLP English correctness probes at each extracted layer for both models.
33	      Apply all 5 transfer conditions across 20 languages: (a) zero-shot, (b) mean-shift
34	      alignment, (c) linear projection, (d) few-shot (25-100 examples), (e) CaCLR.
35	      Implement CaCLR with hyperparameter tuning on held-out English + 5-language
36	      cross-lingual validation set. Phase C — Ablations & Analysis (weeks 6-7): Difficulty-controlled

38	      correctness probes on residuals, test transfer under all conditions — focused
39	      on 10 representative languages × 8 representative layers per model (spanning
40	      20-90% depth). Full Pareto frontier mapping and visualization. Evaluation on
41	      MMLU-ProX (20 languages), Belebele (20 languages), GlobalMMLU (20 languages).
42	      Orthogonality analysis: correctness vs. verbalized confidence direction in non-English

49	      (94 layers, MoE, FP16; 24 probed layers) and Llama 4 Scout (48 layers, MoE,
50	      INT8 weight quantization / FP16 activations; 12 probed layers) on English QA
51	      tasks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge) with known correctness labels. Also extract activations
52	      for a parallel non-English subset (using GlobalMMLU''s matched questions) in
53	      20 languages at the same layers, to enable alignment computation. Store activations

56	      dense, FP16; 15 probed layers) and expand to 50+ languages. Resource Note on
57	      INT8 for Llama 4 Scout: INT8 weight quantization (W8A16) reduces memory from

95	      optimizes for English correctness prediction AND cross-lingual calibration invariance,
96	      transforming the paper from pure empirical characterization into a proposed
97	      method + characterization. Formulation: L_CaCLR = L_BCE(probe(h_en), y_en) +

163	      < 0.04; Miao & Ungar, arXiv 2603.25052), meaning softmax-based approaches —

166	      We propose extracting the linear correctness direction from English intermediate-layer

169	
170	      This work addresses a fundamental scientific question: **what proportion of
171	      the LLM''s cross-lingual correctness transfer is driven by shared difficulty
172	      encoding versus shared capability representations?** Prior work has shown that
173	      knowledge-boundary recognition (an input-level property: is this question answerable?)
174	      transfers cross-lingually (Xiao et al., ACL 2025, arXiv 2504.13816) and difficulty
175	      encoding is cross-lingually shared (Civelli et al., arXiv 2601.12731). Correctness
176	      — an output-dependent property: did the model actually produce the right answer?
177	      — is fundamentally harder, as it combines difficulty, per-language capability,
178	      and representation quality. Rather than asking the binary question "does correctness
179	      transfer?", we quantitatively decompose the transferred signal into its difficulty-shared
180	      and capability-specific components, yielding insight regardless of whether transfer
181	      succeeds or fails.

184	      Our contributions are fourfold. **(1) Pareto Frontier Characterization:** we
185	      map the full frontier of layer depth × calibration quality × cross-lingual transfer
186	      quality across three architectures — Qwen3-235B-A22B (94 layers, MoE), Llama
187	      4 Scout (48 layers, MoE), and Qwen3-32B Dense (64 layers, dense) — and 20 typologically
188	      diverse languages (selected via Ploeger et al.''s principled framework spanning
189	      10+ language families and 3 resource tiers; extended to 50+ in camera-ready)
190	      under five transfer conditions. The inclusion of both MoE and dense architectures
191	      from the same model family (Qwen3) is essential: MoE models exhibit language
192	      routing isolation where high- and low-resource languages activate disjoint expert
193	      subsets (arXiv 2604.03592; arXiv 2510.04694), which could confound Pareto frontier
194	      analysis. The dense model serves as an architectural control. Camera-ready adds
195	      Gemma 4 31B Dense (60 layers). **(2) CaCLR — Calibration-Aware Cross-Lingual
196	      Regularization:** a novel probe training objective that jointly optimizes English
197	      correctness prediction, differentiable calibration quality (via SB-ECE; Karandikar
198	      et al., NeurIPS 2021), and cross-lingual output consistency on aligned non-English
199	      activations. CaCLR addresses a specific identified problem: correctness probes
200	      degrade under distribution shift. CORAL (Miao et al., arXiv 2602.06022, ICML
201	      2026) demonstrated this degradation in cross-task settings but only mitigated
202	      it via weight decay regularization; CaCLR provides a principled solution by
203	      internalizing the target-distribution alignment during training via the consistency
204	      term. CaCLR requires only parallel activations (no non-English correctness labels)
205	      — a supervision requirement qualitatively different from LACE''s per-language
206	      correctness labels: we distinguish three levels: (i) per-language correctness
207	      labels (LACE), (ii) parallel data without labels (CaCLR), (iii) zero-shot (mean-shift
208	      alignment). **(3) Difficulty-Controlled Decomposition:** by projecting out the
209	      IRT difficulty direction (per Civelli et al., 2026) from activations before
210	      training correctness probes, we quantitatively decompose the transferred correctness
211	      signal into a difficulty component (inherently cross-lingual) and a capability
212	      component (language-specific). This decomposition is the scientific core of
213	      the paper: it reveals not just whether transfer works, but why. We validate
214	      the difficulty direction cross-domain (AMC math → MMLU general QA) via cosine
215	      similarity with MMLU-native empirical difficulty probes. **(4) Cross-Lingual
216	      Orthogonality Diagnostics:** we systematically measure whether the orthogonality
217	      between correctness direction and verbalized confidence direction (Miao & Ungar,
218	      2026; English 7-8B models) holds in non-English settings. Zhao et al. (arXiv
219	      2604.01457) identified specific middle-to-late layer circuits responsible for
220	      confidence inflation; if these circuits behave differently across languages,
221	      orthogonality patterns should vary, revealing structural reasons why output-based
222	      calibration fails differently per language.

226	      correctness (output-dependent: did the model answer correctly?) vs. knowledge
227	      boundaries (input-level: is the question answerable?); (2) calibration metrics
228	      (ECE, Brier) vs. classification accuracy; (3) Pareto frontier + CaCLR vs. single-condition
229	      transfer; (4) 20 languages on standard QA vs. 8 on specialized datasets; (5)

244	      ## Core Problem
245	
246	      Non-English languages suffer from 5x worse calibration error (ECE) compared
247	      to English in multilingual LLMs (Zhou et al., LACE). Existing fixes require
248	      per-language correctness labels (LACE) or 5x inference cost (MKA). Output-based
249	      calibration — including temperature scaling and verbalized confidence — is fundamentally
250	      limited by a structural constraint: the model''s internal accuracy estimate
251	      and its verbalized confidence occupy orthogonal subspaces (cosine similarity
252	      < 0.04; Miao & Ungar, 2026). Temperature scaling adjusts a signal that is structurally
253	      decoupled from actual correctness; it cannot close this gap regardless of how
254	      much target-language data is used for fitting.
255	
256	
257	      This paper asks: **of the correctness signal that can be transferred cross-lingually
258	      via intermediate-layer probes, how much is attributable to shared difficulty
259	      encoding (inherently language-agnostic) versus shared capability representations
260	      (a deeper form of meta-cognitive alignment)?** Knowledge boundaries transfer
261	      cross-lingually (Xiao et al., ACL 2025); difficulty encoding is shared (Civelli
262	      et al., 2026). But these are input-level properties. Correctness is output-dependent
263	      — it reflects not just what the model could know, but what it actually produced.
264	      Decomposing the transferred correctness signal reveals the structure of multilingual
265	      LLM meta-cognition.

    approach: 'SCOPING STRATEGY — PHASED SUBMISSION PLAN: Given the EACL 2027 ARR
      deadline of August 3, 2026 (10.5 weeks), we adopt a two-tier approach. The CORE
      SUBMISSION targets 2 models (Qwen3-235B-A22B + Llama 4 Scout) × 20 typologically
      diverse languages × all 5 transfer conditions, producing all three core contributions.
      The CAMERA-READY EXTENSION adds Gemma 4 31B Dense as a third architecture +
      30+ additional languages. This is scientifically justified: 2 models already
      provide architectural contrast (94-layer MoE vs. 48-layer MoE), while the third
      (60-layer dense) strengthens but is not essential for the core claims. LANGUAGE
      SELECTION: Following Ploeger et al.''s (Computational Linguistics, 2025) principled
      framework for typologically diverse language selection, we select 20 languages
      across 3 resource tiers and 10+ language families, constrained to the intersection
      of GlobalMMLU, Belebele, and MMLU-ProX availability: HIGH-RESOURCE (6): Chinese
      (zh), Spanish (es), French (fr), German (de), Japanese (ja), Arabic (ar) — covering
      Sino-Tibetan, Romance, Germanic, Japonic, Afro-Asiatic; MID-RESOURCE (7): Hindi
      (hi), Russian (ru), Korean (ko), Turkish (tr), Vietnamese (vi), Thai (th), Indonesian
      (id) — covering Indo-Aryan, Slavic, Koreanic, Turkic, Austroasiatic, Kra-Dai,
      Austronesian; LOW-RESOURCE (7): Swahili (sw), Bengali (bn), Telugu (te), Khmer
      (km), Yoruba (yo), Amharic (am), Burmese (my) — covering Bantu, Indo-Aryan,
      Dravidian, Austroasiatic, Niger-Congo, Semitic, Sino-Tibetan. This selection
      maximizes typological diversity (word order, morphological type, script diversity)
      while ensuring benchmark coverage and enabling fine-grained resource-tier analysis.
      MINIMAL VIABLE EXPERIMENT (MVE) — 8-WEEK PLAN: Phase A — Infrastructure & Activation
      Extraction (weeks 1-2): Set up extraction pipeline. Extract activations for
      Qwen3-235B-A22B at every 4th layer (24 probed layers across 94 total) and Llama
      4 Scout at every 4th layer (12 probed layers across 48 total) on English MMLU/ARC-Challenge
      with correctness labels + parallel non-English subset for 20 languages using
      GlobalMMLU''s matched questions. INT8 validation ablation for Llama 4 Scout
      on 5% random subset comparing INT8 vs. FP16 at 5 representative layers. Phase
      B — Probe Training & Transfer Experiments (weeks 3-5): Train logistic regression
      + 2-layer MLP English correctness probes at each extracted layer for both models.
      Apply all 5 transfer conditions across 20 languages: (a) zero-shot, (b) mean-shift
      alignment, (c) linear projection, (d) few-shot (25-100 examples), (e) CaCLR.
      Implement CaCLR with hyperparameter tuning on held-out English + 5-language
      cross-lingual validation set. Phase C — Ablations & Analysis (weeks 6-7): Difficulty-controlled
      ablation: train IRT difficulty probes, project out difficulty direction, retrain
      correctness probes on residuals, test transfer under all conditions — focused
      on 10 representative languages × 8 representative layers per model (spanning
      20-90% depth). Full Pareto frontier mapping and visualization. Evaluation on
      MMLU-ProX (20 languages), Belebele (20 languages), GlobalMMLU (20 languages).
      Orthogonality analysis: correctness vs. verbalized confidence direction in non-English
      settings. Phase D — Writing (weeks 8-10.5): Draft paper with 2.5-week buffer
      to deadline. PRIORITY ORDER if time-constrained: (1) Pareto frontier for Qwen3
      + Llama 4 Scout with zero-shot + mean-shift + CaCLR (minimum compelling result);
      (2) add linear projection + few-shot conditions; (3) add difficulty ablation;
      (4) add remaining evaluation benchmarks. Phase 1 — Activation Extraction: Extract
      intermediate-layer activations at every 4th layer across the full depth of Qwen3-235B-A22B
      (94 layers, MoE, FP16; 24 probed layers) and Llama 4 Scout (48 layers, MoE,
      INT8 weight quantization / FP16 activations; 12 probed layers) on English QA
      tasks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge) with known correctness labels. Also extract activations
      for a parallel non-English subset (using GlobalMMLU''s matched questions) in
      20 languages at the same layers, to enable alignment computation. Store activations
      for all layers to enable the full Pareto frontier analysis. For the camera-ready
      extension, additionally extract activations for Gemma 4 31B Dense (60 layers,
      dense, FP16; 15 probed layers) and expand to 50+ languages. Resource Note on
      INT8 for Llama 4 Scout: INT8 weight quantization (W8A16) reduces memory from
      ~220GB (3-4 A100s at FP16) to ~109GB (2 A100-80GBs), while activations are still
      computed and extracted in FP16/BF16, preserving hidden-state fidelity. We validate
      this choice with an ablation on a random 5% subset comparing INT8 vs FP16 probing
      results at 5 representative layers — prior work shows INT8 quantization has
      minimal effect on confidence and calibration properties (Huang et al., arXiv
      2508.16785), with 1-3% accuracy degradation, and middle layers (where we primarily
      probe) show minimal dead-neuron perturbation. Phase 2 — English Probe Training:
      At each extracted layer, fit both a logistic regression probe (linear) and a
      lightweight 2-layer MLP probe to identify the correctness direction — the hyperplane
      or surface best separating correct from incorrect answers in representation
      space. We explicitly note, following Miao & Ungar (2026), that we probe the
      CORRECTNESS direction (= their ''gold calibration direction'': the model''s
      internal estimate of whether it answered correctly), NOT the verbalized confidence
      direction — these are orthogonal (cosine similarity < 0.04) and we target the
      former because it is the true calibration-relevant signal. Compare probe complexity:
      linear probes may transfer better cross-lingually (by analogy to the shallow-transferable
      finding in Civelli et al.), while MLPs may capture richer correctness signals
      (as CORAL found). Phase 3 — Pareto Frontier Analysis (Core Contribution 1):
      Apply each layer''s English-trained probe to non-English activations across
      20 languages (core) / 50+ languages (camera-ready) under five transfer conditions:
      (a) zero-shot (direct application), (b) mean-shift alignment (compute delta-mu
      between English and target-language activation means, shift target activations;
      per Xiao et al., ACL 2025), (c) linear projection alignment (learn least-squares
      projection from small parallel set; per Xiao et al., ACL 2025), (d) few-shot
      probe fine-tuning (25-100 target-language examples; motivated by Confidence
      Manifold''s finding that 25 examples achieve 89% of full-data accuracy), and
      (e) CaCLR — Calibration-Aware Cross-Lingual Regularization (see Phase 3e). For
      each layer x transfer condition, measure (i) calibration quality (ECE, Brier
      score) and (ii) cross-lingual transfer quality (AUROC degradation from English).
      Map the full Pareto frontier of layer depth x calibration quality x cross-lingual
      transferability for each transfer condition and each model. Critically, given
      that optimal cross-lingual transfer depth varies from 24% (Qwen3-8B) to 49%
      (LLaMA-3.1-8B) for difficulty probes, we test whether correctness probes show
      a similar architecture-dependent pattern, and whether alignment techniques flatten
      this variance by enabling effective transfer at deeper, better-calibrated layers.
      Phase 3e — CaCLR: Calibration-Aware Cross-Lingual Regularization (Core Contribution
      2 — Methodological): CaCLR is a novel probe training objective that jointly
      optimizes for English correctness prediction AND cross-lingual calibration invariance,
      transforming the paper from pure empirical characterization into a proposed
      method + characterization. Formulation: L_CaCLR = L_BCE(probe(h_en), y_en) +
      alpha * L_SB-ECE(probe(h_en), y_en) + beta * L_consist(probe(h_en), probe(align(h_X))).
      The first term trains the probe to predict English correctness. The second term
      uses SB-ECE — differentiable soft-binned Expected Calibration Error (Karandikar
      et al., NeurIPS 2021), which replaces discrete ECE bins with temperature-parameterized
      soft membership functions enabling gradient-based optimization — to explicitly
      optimize English calibration during training, not just post-hoc. The third term
      penalizes divergence between the probe''s outputs on English activations and
      aligned (mean-shifted or projected) non-English activations for parallel questions,
      enforcing cross-lingual output consistency. Crucially, CaCLR requires NO non-English
      correctness labels: the consistency term uses only parallel activations (available
      from Phase 1), and the SB-ECE term operates on English data only. The key hypothesis:
      by jointly optimizing calibration quality (via SB-ECE) and cross-lingual invariance
      (via consistency), CaCLR produces probes that transfer calibration more effectively
      than probes trained with standard BCE loss alone, particularly at deeper layers
      where calibration is superior but zero-shot transfer fails. We compare CaCLR-trained
      probes against conditions (a)-(d) across the full Pareto frontier. Hyperparameters
      alpha and beta are tuned on a held-out English validation set with a small (5-language)
      cross-lingual validation set. Phase 4 — Frontier Shifting Analysis: Quantify
      how each alignment/adaptation technique shifts the Pareto frontier. Key hypotheses:
      (H1) mean-shift and linear projection alignment (which require only unlabeled
      parallel activations, no correctness labels) may enable effective transfer at
      deeper layers where calibration is superior (75-91% depth) but zero-shot transfer
      fails — potentially resolving the depth-transferability tradeoff without requiring
      labeled target-language data; (H2) CaCLR dominates conditions (a)-(c) because
      it internalizes the alignment objective during training, producing inherently
      more transferable probes; (H3) CaCLR + few-shot adaptation achieves the best
      Pareto frontier overall, combining training-time invariance with target-language
      fine-tuning. Compare cost-effectiveness: mean-shift (zero labeled examples,
      needs only activation means) vs. linear projection (zero labeled examples, needs
      small parallel activation set) vs. few-'

    core_problem: 'Non-English languages suffer from 5x worse calibration error (ECE)
      compared to English in multilingual LLMs. Existing fixes require per-language
      validation data (LACE) or expensive multilingual sampling (MKA). Output-based
      calibration methods are further limited by a fundamental representational constraint:
      the model''s internal accuracy estimate and its verbalized confidence occupy
      orthogonal subspaces (cosine similarity < 0.04 across all layers; Miao & Ungar,
      2026), meaning softmax probabilities and prompted confidence scores are structurally
      decoupled from what the model actually knows about its own correctness. While
      recent work has shown that knowledge-boundary recognition (answerable vs. unanswerable)
      can transfer cross-lingually via linear probes at middle layers (Xiao et al.,
      ACL 2025), calibration — the alignment between model confidence and actual correctness
      — is a fundamentally different and harder transfer target: it depends not just
      on what the model knows, but on how its capabilities, representation quality,
      and confidence interact per-language. Can we transfer English calibration quality

      calibration — including temperature scaling and verbalized confidence — is fundamentally
      limited by a structural constraint: the model''s internal accuracy estimate
      and its verbalized confidence occupy orthogonal subspaces (cosine similarity
      < 0.04; Miao & Ungar, 2026). Temperature scaling adjusts a signal that is structurally
      decoupled from actual correctness; it cannot close this gap regardless of how
      much target-language data is used for fitting.


      This paper asks: **of the correctness signal that can be transferred cross-lingually
      via intermediate-layer probes, how much is attributable to shared difficulty
      encoding (inherently language-agnostic) versus shared capability representations
      (a deeper form of meta-cognitive alignment)?** Knowledge boundaries transfer
      cross-lingually (Xiao et al., ACL 2025); difficulty encoding is shared (Civelli
      et al., 2026). But these are input-level properties. Correctness is output-dependent
      — it reflects not just what the model could know, but what it actually produced.
      Decomposing the transferred correctness signal reveals the structure of multilingual

跨语言校准迁移：从英语中间层提取 correctness direction（非 verbalized confidence），迁移到非英语语言改善校准（ECE）。核心科学问题：迁移的 correctness 信号中，difficulty-shared vs capability-specific 各占多少？

# xling_calib_direction — Research Dashboard

## 核心方向
跨语言校准迁移：从英语中间层提取 correctness direction（非 verbalized confidence），迁移到非英语语言改善校准（ECE）。核心科学问题：迁移的 correctness 信号中，difficulty-shared vs capability-specific 各占多少？

## 当前阶段：MVP 验证

**核心假设**：英语中间层训练的 correctness probe 可以 zero-shot 或经简单对齐后迁移到非英语，在非英语上产生优于 temperature scaling 的校准效果。

**MVP 设计**：
- 模型：Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct（Miao & Ungar 2026 三个验证模型之一）
- 数据：MMLU 英语 + GlobalMMLU 4 非英语（zh/es/hi/sw，覆盖 high/mid/low resource）
- 层：每隔 4 层（~7 层，20%-90% 深度）
- Probe：logistic regression + 2-layer MLP（并行跑，成本可忽略）
- 迁移：zero-shot + mean-shift alignment（mean-shift 用 100 samples 目标语言激活计算均值，无需标注）
- Baseline：final-layer softmax + temperature scaling（temp scaling 为主要对比标准）

**Pass/Fail 标准**（D002 修订）：
- **PASS**：任一 probe 英语 AUROC > 0.65 AND ≥2/4 非英语在某层迁移后 ECE 优于 temp scaling ≥1pp
- **CONDITIONAL**：AUROC 0.60-0.65 OR 仅 1/4 语言通过 → 升级到 Qwen2.5-14B 复测
- **FAIL**：最优 probe 英语 AUROC < 0.60 OR 无语言优于 temp scaling

## 近期任务
- [ ] 用户配置 GPU 服务器
- [ ] Agent 搭建环境 + 下载 Qwen2.5-7B + GlobalMMLU
- [ ] 实现 activation extraction + probe training + 迁移评估 pipeline
- [ ] 分析结果，判断 pass/conditional/fail

## GPU 预算
- MVP：1× A100-80GB 或同级（~5-10 GPU-hours）
- 尚未配置服务器

## 关键风险
1. Correctness 是 output-dependent 信号，可能不如 knowledge-boundary 那样 language-agnostic
2. 7B 模型 representation 不够丰富 → conditional 路径升级到 14B
3. LR 可能漏非线性信号 → MLP 作为 fallback（已纳入 MVP）
